entry.title: Docker Compose
entry.content:
What is Docker Compose?

Docker Compose is a tool that allows users to define multiple Docker containers’ configurations using a YAML file. With a simple command, you can start, stop, and manage all the containers of an entire application, making development and testing more efficient.

Difference Between Docker and Docker Compose

  • Docker: Docker is a platform that allows developers to automate the deployment of applications inside lightweight containers. Each container runs a single application or service, making it easy to package and distribute applications along with their dependencies.

  • Docker Compose: Docker Compose is a tool used to define and manage multi-container applications. It allows users to configure multiple containers in a single YAML file, enabling them to start, stop, and manage all containers with a single command. Docker Compose is particularly useful for applications that require multiple services, such as a web server and a database.

Why Use Docker Compose?

  • Simplified Management: Centralizes the management of multiple container configurations in a YAML file, reducing the complexity of manual operations.
  • Environment Consistency: Ensures that container configurations are consistent across development, testing, and production environments, minimizing issues caused by environmental differences.
  • Scalability: Easily add or remove services to adapt to changing requirements.
  • Automation: Supports one-click startup and shutdown of the entire application, improving development efficiency.

Conclusion

Docker Compose is a powerful tool that helps developers manage and deploy multi-container applications more easily. With a simple YAML configuration, you can quickly start and stop an entire application, enhancing development efficiency and environmental consistency. Whether you are a beginner or an experienced developer, Docker Compose is an indispensable tool in your containerization development process.

entry.title: Docker
entry.content:
Introduction

In today’s fast-paced development environment, the need for efficient software deployment and scalability is paramount. Docker has emerged as a groundbreaking technology that allows developers to easily package, deploy, and manage applications in isolated environments known as containers.

What is Docker?

Docker is an open-source platform that automates the deployment of applications inside lightweight, portable containers. Containers are a standardized unit of software that encapsulate an application and all its dependencies, ensuring that it runs seamlessly across different computing environments.

Why Use Docker?

  1. Portability: Docker containers can run on any machine that has Docker installed, making it easy to move applications between development, testing, and production environments.

  2. Isolation: Each Docker container runs in its own isolated environment, allowing developers to avoid conflicts between different software libraries and dependencies.

  3. Scalability: Docker enables easy scaling of applications by allowing multiple instances of a container to run simultaneously to handle increased loads.

  4. Efficiency: Containers share the host OS kernel, making them more lightweight than traditional virtual machines, which require a guest OS.

Key Concepts in Docker

  1. Images vs. Containers:

    • Image: A Docker image is a read-only template used to create containers. Images contain the application code, libraries, and environment variables.
    • Container: A container is a running instance of an image. It is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software.

  2. Dockerfile:
    A Dockerfile is a script containing a series of instructions to create a Docker image. It defines everything required to set up an application, including the base image, dependencies, and configuration settings.

  3. Docker Hub:
    Docker Hub is a cloud-based repository where developers can store and share Docker images. It provides a platform to find pre-built images and collaborate with other developers.

Getting Started with Docker

Conclusion

Docker is revolutionizing the way software is developed and deployed by promoting portability, scalability, and efficiency. With its growing ecosystem and robust community support, Docker is becoming a standard tool for developers worldwide. Embracing Docker can significantly enhance your development workflow and lead to more reliable and consistent application deployments.

Use Official Base Images

Start with official images from Docker Hub when possible. They are optimized and maintained by the community.

Image Tag Table Comparison

Tag Description Base OS Size Use Case
python:3.9 Official Python 3.9 image. Debian-based Larger General-purpose Python applications.
python:3.9-slim Slimmed down version of Python 3.9. Debian-based Smaller Lightweight applications, reduced image size.

python:3.10-slim Slimmed down version of Python 3.10. Debian-based Smaller Lightweight applications, reduced image size.

python:-bullseye Python image based on Debian Bullseye (e.g., python:3.9-bullseye). Debian Bullseye Medium Applications needing Debian Bullseye compatibility.

Minimize Layers

Combine commands to reduce the number of layers in your image. Use && to chain commands together.

Leverage Caching

Order your commands to take advantage of Docker’s caching mechanism. Place less frequently changing commands (like installing dependencies) at the top.

Use .dockerignore

Create a .dockerignore file to exclude unnecessary files from being copied into the image, which can help reduce the image size.

Specify a Non-Root User

For security reasons, run your application as a non-root user.

Keep Images Small

Use lighter base images (like alpine) and remove unnecessary files after installation to keep your image size small.

Use Multi-Stage Builds

For complex applications, use multi-stage builds to separate the build environment from the runtime environment.

Set Environment Variables

Use ENV to define environment variables that can be reused throughout the Dockerfile.

entry.title: Project Management - Five Process Group
entry.content:
Five Process Group

The five main processes are initiation, planning, execution, monitoring, and closure. The following events occur in the five main processes:

No Process Group Description
1 Initiating Define and authorize the project. Identify the Business Case.
2 Planning Define and refine goals, plan action steps.
3 Executing Integrate manpower and resources to carry out the project.
4 Monitoring and Controlling Regularly measure and monitor progress to control the project and achieve goals.
5 Closing Ensure that the products, services, or results of the project are accepted, and orderly close the project.

Project Life Cycle

In the early stages of a project, stakeholders have a significant influence on the direction of the project, and the cost of changes is relatively low. However, as the project progresses to later stages, stakeholders’ ability to influence decreases, and the cost of changes increases. In simple terms, this is the concept of “the ship has sailed.”

It’s important to note that a decrease in influence over the project’s direction does not mean a decrease in influence over the project’s success or failure. Discontented individuals can still easily cause the project to fail.

Common Tools

Goal Setting

Having goals provides direction; without goals or with too many goals, it is difficult to reach a consensus. Goals should be limited to three, prioritized accordingly, and must meet the SMART criteria. Many people say that leisure is a goal, but leisure can serve various purposes such as resting, experiencing different lifestyles, connecting with others, and meeting new people, etc. Different goals will generate different action plans.

Business Case

All projects must be cost-effective. Are the products, services, and results generated by the project worth our time and effort?

Common Misconceptions

Goals cannot be changed

As long as the sponsor agrees, goals can be changed. Of course, each time a goal is modified, the team will need some time to refocus, which is something to be mindful of.

Plans cannot change

If we could control the weather and prevent illness, then plans could certainly remain unchanged. Unfortunately, we are neither gods nor can we control the environment. When circumstances change, it is natural to adjust plans. Just like when the wind changes direction, if we do not adjust the sails, will we reach our destination?

However, changing plans can be painful, especially after a lot of preparation and processes have been set. This is why agile project management is becoming popular in frequently changing environments. Agile methods emphasize short iterations to avoid spending excessive time on plans that are bound to change. Nevertheless, it is still necessary to set mid-to-long-term goals to serve as a direction.

entry.title: Project Management - Stackholder
entry.content:
Roles in Project Management

In the framework of software management, there are four roles in running a project:

1. Project Sponsor

Quantity: One
The person who funds the project, usually a senior manager, holds political responsibility for the project’s success or failure.

2. Project Manager (PM)

Quantity: One
The person who actually runs and monitors the project, holding direct responsibility for its success or failure.

3. Project Team

Quantity: Several to many
Those who participate in the project.

4. Stakeholders

Quantity: A truckload to countless
Everyone who has a say in the project.

4 Steps to Create a Project Stakeholder Analysis Diagram

Identifying and managing your project stakeholders is an excellent way to lay the foundation for a successful project. When key project stakeholders trust you, they are more likely to provide support, which can be crucial throughout the project lifecycle. Conversely, without supportive stakeholders, you may find yourself having to set stakeholder expectations halfway through the project, which can lead to changes and unnecessary project risks. To avoid this, you must take the following four steps to create an effective project stakeholder analysis diagram.

Step 1: Identify Project Stakeholders

Before managing stakeholder expectations, you first need to know who the stakeholders are. Be sure to include both internal and external stakeholders. To figure out who your project stakeholders are, ask yourself:

  • Who cares about this project?
  • Who will be affected by this project?
  • Who can influence this project?
  • Who can approve/reject this project?

Step 2: Determine the Influence and Interest Levels of Project Stakeholders

If high-level project stakeholders participate, they can truly elevate your project to a higher level. The best way to confirm high-level involvement is to establish a clear stakeholder analysis diagram that outlines the influence and interest levels of each project stakeholder. This matrix structure (sometimes referred to as the power-interest matrix) is the best way to visually represent the four main groups of project stakeholders.

The four main groups of project stakeholders are:

  1. High Influence and High Interest: Manage Closely
  2. High Influence and Low Interest: Keep Satisfied
  3. Low Influence and High Interest: Keep Informed
  4. Low Influence and Low Interest: Monitor

Step 3: Understand Stakeholder Needs

The reality is that some stakeholders may disagree with specific elements of the project. As a project manager, you are responsible for understanding their needs and perspectives, and finding solutions that will not negatively impact the success of the project. You are not obligated to do everything that stakeholders ask of you, but you are obligated to listen to and understand their needs.

Sometimes, certain individuals may seem like “difficult stakeholders,” but in fact, their priorities may simply differ from yours. Your work might even interrupt parts of their workflow. If you try to see things from their perspective, you will have a better chance of finding solutions and turning the situation into a win-win outcome.

When in doubt, put yourself in others’ shoes. Ask yourself:

  • What do they need?
  • What level of communication do they want?
  • What is the most effective communication strategy?
  • Do these stakeholders have anyone they influence, or are they influenced by others?
  • How do you accurately identify the interests of stakeholders?

Step 4: Include Project Stakeholders in the Recipient List

Once you have identified your project stakeholders and considered their needs, it is essential to invite them to participate in project planning workshops and kickoff meetings (if applicable). Key project stakeholders should also sign off on the project charter, project plan, project objectives, and project scope.

Common Myths

  1. Every stakeholder needs to be satisfied.
    Stakeholder management involves categorization, allowing us to focus our efforts where they matter most and avoid the dilemma of trying to please everyone.

  2. Stakeholders only need to be dealt with.
    Valuable insights and details that can significantly impact the success or failure of a project can be gained from stakeholders. Properly utilizing these insights can lead to smoother project execution.

entry.title: Project Management - Time Management
entry.content:
Waterfull

Milestone

Some activities are far more important and representative than others, so we treat them as milestones to see how far we are from our plans. Examples include graduating from college, getting married, having children, starting a business, and retiring.

Rolling Wave Planning

This is probably the term in PMBOK that is closest to Agile. It uses a method of Progressive Elaboration, where we plan in detail and specifically for the near term, while keeping the long-term plans rough and abstract. For instance, at the age of twelve, one might think about how to study in junior high school to best benefit their future and establish specific plans, whereas thinking about the details of marriage or college right now may simply be speculative and a waste of time.

Schedule Compression

Under the premise of not changing the project scope, the goal is to shorten the overall duration of the project. There are two common methods:

  1. Crashing: This means spending money to buy time, such as hiring an excellent tutor to make courses easier to understand. Or, in the case of marriage, offering a bride price and a house to reduce the time spent finding a girlfriend. It’s important to note that while the project timeline may shorten, the goal may not be achieved. For instance, if the original intention was to find someone who loves you for marriage, it might change to seeking someone who loves money instead. However, if the only goal is to get married to anyone, then it doesn’t matter.

  2. Fast Tracking: This involves changing originally sequential activities to be carried out in parallel. A common example is a part-time job while studying, or studying at university while having children. Typically, the cost of Fast Tracking is an increased risk, as proceeding before the right time can

Common way to estimate the time

  1. Expert Judgment: Consult familiar team members or external experts for evaluations.
  2. Analogous Estimation: Estimate time based on similar past projects.
  3. Parametric Estimation: Use historical data parameters for calculations, suitable for simple tasks. For example, cabinet installation time is estimated using dimensions, but higher carpentry complexity increases variability.
  4. Three-Point Estimation: Divide estimates into “most likely,” “pessimistic,” and “optimistic” values, useful for projects with risks and uncertainties.
  5. Bottom-Up Estimation: Start estimating from the lowest Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) level and accumulate upwards.

Scrum

Story Points Represent: “Time Scale” of Tasks

"People actually do not have much ability to estimate the time required for big tasks."

Each Sprint may contain dozens of Stories, and each Story has its own Story Point used to measure the “time scale” of a single task. The assessment of the time scale includes factors such as “complexity,” “number of people involved,” “familiarity,” “difficulty,” and “basic operation time.” Generally, the more complex the task, the more people involved, and the less familiar it is… the more time it will take.

Since it is a measure of “time scale,” it, of course, “excludes” the value brought by completing the task, the money that needs to be spent, and so on.

Simple Process for Story Point Estimation

Estimating story points is similar to a simple show of hands. Here’s our company’s process:

  1. Complete Story Overview:
    Begin the planning meeting by discussing all aspects of the stories (goals, methods, criteria, etc.).

  2. Establish Criteria for Evaluation:
    Set foundational standards using a couple of stories to create a consensus. For example, if you think a story is a 5-point and I think it’s a 13-point, we aim to adjust them to a common team score, like a 5.

  3. Individual Scoring:
    Members score the stories independently on a form using Fibonacci numbers (1-21). This is done silently, without discussion or questions. After everyone has submitted their scores, discussion can begin.

    (If there are issues, use “?” or “21” to highlight concerns, as asking questions afterward would be redundant.)

  4. Discuss Significant Discrepancies:
    Focus on stories with large differences in scores where consensus is not reached.

entry.title: Project Management
entry.content:
Pareto principle (80/20 principle)

Productivity

You can use the 80/20 rule to prioritize the tasks that must be completed first during the day.
The concept is that by completing the 20% of tasks on your entire task list that should be prioritized, you can achieve 80% of your daily work results. Therefore, to accomplish the most impactful work, you should identify which tasks have the greatest impact on the team and focus your efforts on those tasks throughout the day.

Descsion making

Suppose you work at an e-commerce company. You have reviewed 100 recent customer service complaints and found that most of the complaints were due to customers receiving damaged products. After calculating the amount of refunds your team has issued for damaged products, you discovered that 80% of the refunds given were for damaged products. Your company wants to prevent the operations related to providing refunds for damaged products, so you view this issue as a priority solution.

Sufficiency of Information for Requirements

What problems are currently being encountered?
What possible solutions could there be?
What benefits will come from solving this problem, or what difficulties will it resolve?

Requirement Analysis

  • Clarify the purpose of requirements: Understand the business objectives and user needs behind the requirements, such as whether to improve conversion rates, enhance user experience, or increase user numbers.
  • Define business value: Quantify the impact of requirements on business value, such as revenue increase, cost reduction, and heightened user engagement. Business value helps stakeholders understand the importance of the requirements.
  • Technical feasibility assessment: Collaborate with the technical team to analyze the technical challenges of the requirements, including development complexity, system compatibility, and feasibility. This can help all parties evaluate implementation costs and risks.

80/20法則

生產力
您可以使用 80/20 法則來優先執行一天當中必須先完成的任務。

其概念是完成整個任務清單中 20% 最應優先執行的任務，就能為您當天的工作成果帶來 80% 的影響。有鑑於此，若要完成最具影響力的工作，就應辨別哪些任務對團隊有最大的影響，並在一天當中專心投入這些任務。

做決策
假設您在一家電子商務公司工作。您看了近期有關客戶服務的 100 份投訴，並且發現大部分的投訴原因是客戶收到破損產品。您的團隊針對破損產品而提供退款的金額做了計算後，發現給出去的退款中有 80% 是用在破損產品的退款。您的公司想要防止為破損產品提供退款的相關作業，因此您將這個問題視為優先執行的解決方案。

需求的資訊充足性

  • 目前遇到什麼問題？
  • 可能可以有什麼解法？
  • 這個問題解決後，會帶來什麼好處，或者解決哪些困難？

最典型的 user story 公式就是：作為 {某種使用者} (Who)，我想要 {做到某件事}(What)，這樣我就可以 {達到什麼目標}(Why)。

需求分析

  • 明確需求目的：了解需求背後的業務目標和使用者需求，例如是否提高轉換率、提升使用體驗或增加用戶數。
  • 定義商業價值：將需求對商業價值進行量化，例如收入增加、成本降低、使用者黏性提升等。商業價值有助於利益相關者理解需求的重要性。
  • 技術可行性評估：與技術團隊合作，分析需求的技術挑戰，包括開發複雜度、系統兼容性和可行性。這樣可以幫助各方評估實施成本和風險。

Understanding Pytest Fixtures: A Comprehensive Guide

What is a Fixture?

A fixture in pytest is a function that sets up some context or state for your tests. It allows you to create reusable test setups, reducing code duplication and improving test clarity. Fixtures can manage resources like database connections, file handles, or any other setup needed for your tests.

Defining Fixtures

To define a fixture, use the @pytest.fixture decorator. Here’s a simple example:

Using Fixtures in Tests

You can use a fixture by including it as an argument in your test function:

Fixture Scope

Fixtures can have different scopes that determine how often they are invoked:

  • function: Each function or method is called.
  • class: Each class is called once; a class can have multiple methods.
  • module: Each .py file is called once; the file contains multiple functions and classes.
  • session: Multiple files are called once, can be called across .py files; each .py file is a module.

  1. Function Scope (Default)
    This is the default scope. The fixture is invoked for each test function that uses it.

    Output:

  2. Class Scope
    When the fixture is at the class level, if multiple test cases in a class call this fixture, then this fixture is executed only once before all the test cases in that class start.

    Output:

  3. Module Scope
    When the fixture is at the module level, it only runs once before all tests in the current .py script start.

    Output:

  4. Session Scope
    A session-scoped fixture can be used across multiple .py modules. If several test cases only need to call the fixture once, set it in the conftest.py file. This file is automatically recognized by pytest. Placing it in the project root allows global access, while placing it in a specific package limits its use to that package.

    Output:

Yielding Fixtures

Using yield in fixtures allows you to separate setup and teardown logic. Code before yield runs before the test, and code after runs after:

Parameterized Fixtures

Parameterized fixtures allow you to run a test with multiple sets of data:

Autouse Fixtures

If you want a fixture to be automatically used by tests without explicitly including it, set autouse=True:

Best Practices for Using Fixtures

  1. Keep Fixtures Focused: Each fixture should handle a specific setup. This makes them easier to understand and reuse.
  2. Use Descriptive Names: Name your fixtures clearly to indicate their purpose.
  3. Avoid Global State: Ensure your fixtures do not rely on or modify global state to prevent side effects in tests.
  4. Combine Fixtures: You can use multiple fixtures in a single test by including them as parameters.

Conclusion

Fixtures are an essential feature in pytest that can greatly enhance your testing strategy. By leveraging fixtures, you can write cleaner, more maintainable tests while reducing redundancy. For further exploration, refer to the official pytest documentation.

A Beginner’s Guide to Python Unit Testing with Pytest

Unit testing is an essential practice in software development that helps ensure your code behaves as expected. This guide will introduce you to the basics of unit testing in Python using the pytest framework.

What is Unit Testing?

Unit testing involves testing individual components of your code (usually functions or classes) to verify that they work correctly. This practice helps catch bugs early and makes your code more maintainable.

Why Unit Test?

  • Catch Bugs Early: Identify issues before they become larger problems.
  • Simplify Integration: Ensure that each part of your code works independently.
  • Facilitate Refactoring: Make changes to your code with confidence that existing functionality is preserved.
  • Documentation: Provide examples of how your code is intended to be used.

Introducing Pytest

pytest is a popular testing framework for Python that makes it easy to write simple and scalable test cases. It offers powerful features like fixtures, parameterized testing, and a rich ecosystem of plugins.

Installing Pytest

Best Practices for Unit Testing with Pytest

Conclusion
